<h3 align="center">CASTAWAY <sub><i>(working title)</i></sub></h3>

<p align="center">
  <b>Ten hours on one very small island. She stays. Everything else drifts by.</b><br>
  She idles, nodding to the music on her headphones. Every so often something happens, and quite often it arrives by sea.
</p>

<p align="center">
  <kbd>DYCP</kbd> every character at its own height
  &nbsp;·&nbsp;
  <kbd>HER</kbd> sand level, mostly
  &nbsp;·&nbsp;
  <kbd>SAMPLES</kbd> 0
</p>

**Castaway** is a stationary-frame lo-fi video for YouTube, in the spirit of the ten-hour lofi streams: a young woman alone on a tiny island with one tall palm, a raft and a lot of time. She mostly idles. Every so often, a message in a bottle washes straight back, a stray cat arrives on a crate and naps up the palm, or a shark in headphones surfaces and nods to the beat. It is an unofficial remake inspired by the small-island routines and visual comedy of *Johnny Castaway*, the 1992 desert-island screensaver, repainted in a sunny, hand-painted coastal anime style: 16:9, 1080p, 30 fps, and always daytime.

[activities.toml](activities.toml) holds more than 90 activities on four timers, from a coconut every few minutes to "she could leave any time" once in a very long while. Every one of them starts on the next bar of the music, so the gags land on the beat. Every sound is synthesized from code by [tools/make_audio.py](tools/make_audio.py): no samples, no loops, no recordings.

```sh
python tools/serve.py
# then open http://127.0.0.1:8765/
```

The page plays a live preview and exports a YouTube-ready MP4. In development: no video has been published yet, so for now the only way to watch her wait is to run it.

<details>
<summary><b>THE CHARSET</b>: what drifts past in the scroller, and how often it really does</summary>

```text
 THE CHARSET: 8x8 CAPITALS, ONE QUAVER, FIVE SPRITES THAT FLOAT
 ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  SPRITE            IN THE VIDEO                            TIMER
  green bottle .... her message, washed straight back ..... occasional
  cat on a crate .. grey tabby, naps up the palm, leaves .. rare
  sea turtle ...... swims in, dozes off beside her ........ occasional
  shark ........... surfaces in headphones, nods along .... rare
  walking coconut . lands on a hermit crab, walks off ..... occasional
 ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  OCCASIONAL: every 12 to 25 minutes   RARE: every 30 to 60 minutes
```

In the banner they come round every two minutes or so. In the video, each timer picks one activity from its tier when it goes off, and the occasional tier is crowded, so in any one ten-hour run some of these will not come round at all. A different bottle brings a reply to hers, hours later. The cat comes back another time. The scroller has no room for that much patience; she has plenty.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>THE SCHEDULE</b>: four timers, ten hours, about two hundred things</summary>

```text
 TIER ......... COMES ROUND ......... IN A TYPICAL TEN-HOUR RUN
 REGULAR ...... every 2 to 5 min .... about 155 (coconut, fishing, laps)
 OCCASIONAL ... every 12 to 25 min .. about 30
 RARE ......... every 30 to 60 min .. about 13
 SUPER RARE ... every 3 to 6 hours .. about 2, at most 3
 CHAINED ...... never on a timer .... the tide, after each sandcastle
 IDLE ......... the rest ............ about two thirds of the time

 default run: 10:00:00, seed 1992, one bar = 3 s
```

The counts are the median of 200 simulated runs, as the header of [activities.toml](activities.toml) says. Lanes let things overlap, so a ship can sail past while she is busy with a coconut. `python tools/schedule.py` validates the file and simulates a ten-hour run; `python tools/render_demo.py --dev` renders a dev reel of every activity with a heads-up display, from the older Python reference renderer.

The scene has a life of its own too: 26 entries, four always on and 22 timed. Shore waves and drifting cloud shadows are built; distant birds, planes with vapour trails, whale pods, dolphins, sailboats, sandpipers, a gecko and a rain shower are planned. Daytime rain, naturally.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>THE SOUND</b>: synthesized, measured, not yet heard</summary>

Everything comes out of [tools/make_audio.py](tools/make_audio.py), more than 150 files so far, with no samples, loops or recordings, so no third-party licence applies. The theme is a seamless 60-second loop at 80 BPM in F major (ii-V-I-vi): 20 bars of exactly 3 seconds, with electric piano, a kalimba lead, soft drums and vinyl crackle. The ocean ambience is a seamless 60-second loop as well. The mix sits at -14 LUFS with true peak at or below -1 dBTP, and the levels can be set in master and per routine.

Nobody has listened to it yet. It is, technically, still a surprise.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>HOW THE BANNER WORKS</b>: DYCP, FLD, tech-tech, and one sine table</summary>

**DYCP** is Different Y Character Position: the Commodore 64 scroller in which every character of the line sits at its own height, so the text ripples along a sine as it scrolls. Here every letter and sprite is a reference to one shared glyph, and all of them run the same stepped sine track (whole-pixel steps, like a table in memory), each with its own delay, while the whole line slides left. The wave is about 256 pixels long and drifts slowly right, against the text. The letters sit in a mask over fixed bands of colour, so each one turns yellow on a crest and cyan in a trough, the way a raster colour split would do it.

**FLD** pushed whole rows of a screen up and down; here the CAST row hops on the first beat of every bar and AWAY a beat later. **Tech-tech** slid each scanline of a logo sideways; here it is the wave lines of the sea under the island, each one a little behind the line above. The logo letters are fat squared capitals sampled on the multicolour grid (pixels twice as wide as they are tall), filled with a diagonal stripe pattern that cycles one pixel at a time. All sixteen colours are the C64's own, except her skin tone.

The look is the C64 DYCP demo part of 1989 to 1992. The references are Sphinx's *DYCP Mania* (1989), for the striped logo on mauve panels, and The Force's *DYCP Intro* (1991), for the scroller hanging under a two-row logo. They are credited here as the reference; none of their logos, charsets or pictures were copied, and everything in the banner was drawn from scratch by its generator. No script, no GIF, no filters, and with reduced motion switched on, the whole screen holds still on its first frame.

</details>
